source.title_on_document: Human direction drives creativity with large language models

supplement.holds: Scoring rubrics and prompts, expanded sample methods and exclusions, reliability and correlation tables, mediation estimates, and robustness analyses.

paper_design_summary: Four samples relate measured Creative Direction in human–LLM chats to rated product creativity and similarity across outputs: Prolific title/design tasks with GPT-4o, Prolific personal writing with ChatGPT, a separate Prolific Gemini replication, and naturalistic WildChat conversations (pp. 16–18, 33–42). Sample 1 compares AI-assisted and solo work within people and is described as counterbalanced, but random allocation of condition order is not stated; the other samples use common AI access or existing chats and observed Creative Direction rather than assigned direction levels (pp. 18, 33, 35, 37–42). Final outputs were rated for novelty and effectiveness by automated scorers, with human ratings used for validation, and embeddings measured output similarity (pp. 7, 16, 18, 33).

studies.label: Sample 1: counterbalanced ChatGPT-versus-solo title and design tasks; order allocation unstated

assignment.what_was_assigned: Task was crossed with AI chat versus solo condition within participants. The supplement says counterbalanced but does not state how condition orders were allocated or that allocation was random. Creative Direction was measured from chat transcripts.
assignment.quote: Each participant completed two creative tasks in a within-subjects design crossing task with condition (AI chat vs. solo, counterbalanced).
assignment.locator: p. 33, Supplementary Information, Sample 1 Methods: Participants; p. 16, Materials and Methods: Sample 1

arms.name: GPT-4o chat
arms.description: AI-assisted condition in the within-person comparison. Analyzed people are not reported separately for this condition.

arms.name: Solo
arms.description: Unassisted condition in the same within-person comparison. Analyzed people are not reported separately for this condition.

participants.who: Prolific participants; the paper reports an overall analytic N of 234. The 413 retained chat interactions are task observations, not additional participants; per-condition analyzed people are not separately reported.
participants.quote: N = 234 participants were recruited via Prolific.
participants.locator: p. 43, Table S6 (Analytic N); pp. 33–34, Supplementary Information, Sample 1 Methods: Participants; p. 16, Materials and Methods: Sample 1

ai_tool.how_used: Custom browser chat hosted on PythonAnywhere; the system prompt requested brief suggestions rather than full solutions. Participants could exchange prompts and suggestions while preparing their responses (p. 34, LLM Interface).

task.description: Creative title generation for a supplied story excerpt and written ideation of a solution to help people with mobility impairments navigate stairs; both tasks compared AI-assisted and solo outputs (pp. 16, 33–35).

outcomes.name: Product creativity of titles and design solutions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Final product creativity is the mean of GPT-4.1, Qwen 3.5-397B, and Grok-3 ratings on a 10–50 scale anchored by novelty and effectiveness (p. 16, Product Creativity Scoring; pp. 28–29, Product Scoring: Creativity). Creative Direction (CD) is scored separately from the chat transcript by a different ensemble of models; primary correlations use mean CD and mean creativity per participant/user (pp. 16, 18). Creativity is scored in both AI-chat and solo conditions; CD is available only for engaged chat interactions (p. 16, Sample 1).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted versus solo outputs: title generation, paired-samples dz = 0.82; design solutions, paired-samples dz = 2.03; both p < .001. AI-assisted outputs were rated more creative on both tasks. Product creativity was rated on a 10–50 scale anchored by novelty and effectiveness by GPT-4.1, Qwen 3.5-397B, and Grok-3.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Results: LLMs Can Homogenize or Diversify Ideas Depending on the Task; p. 16, Product Creativity Scoring; p. 35, AI vs. Solo Comparisons

contrasts.reported: Within AI-assisted work, person-level measured-CD association: r = .28, N = 234 (p. 7). Table S5 gives zero-order r = +.276 (p < .001) and partial r = +.202 (p = .002), controlling interaction quantity. These are observational correlations, not assigned-treatment effects.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Creative Direction Robustly Predicts Creative Performance; p. 18, Analysis; p. 42, Table S5

outcomes.name: Across-person output similarity in AI-assisted versus solo tasks
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean pairwise cosine similarity is compared between GPT-4o-chat and solo outputs within each task (pp. 10, 35). The homogenization method identifies all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings (pp. 11, 18), but the AI-versus-solo paragraphs do not specify the independent analysis unit or uncertainty procedure.

contrasts.reported: Design task: mean pairwise cosine similarity, chat .500 versus solo .338, d = 1.10 (more homogenized with AI). Title task: chat .255 versus solo .297, d = −0.25 (more diverse with AI). These are the paper's printed similarity effects, without sign reversal. The paragraph does not specify the independent analysis unit for these AI-versus-solo similarity contrasts, so unit is null.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Results: LLMs Can Homogenize or Diversify Ideas Depending on the Task; p. 35, Supplementary Information: AI vs. Solo Comparisons; p. 18, Homogenization Analysis (sentence-transformer cosine similarities)

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity; lower values mean greater across-person diversity.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pairs of GPT-4o-chat outputs compared with other chat outputs, and pairs of solo outputs compared with other solo outputs, within the title and design tasks (pp. 10, 35).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Not stated for the AI-versus-solo contrasts. The independent analysis unit is also unspecified, so unit remains null. Welch tests described for observed-CD groups are not assumed to apply.
diversity_detail.notes: Reported values retain the paper's similarity signs without reversal: design d = 1.10 indicates less diversity with AI; title d = −0.25 indicates more diversity with AI. Direction is therefore mixed. The printed statistics are preserved under the form's instruction not to compute effects.

outcomes.name: Across-person output diversity by measured Creative Direction in title and design tasks
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: AI-assisted title and design outputs enter the observational median-CD comparison. Across Samples 1 and 2, high-CD outputs were significantly less similar in 4 of 6 tasks, but the paper does not print separate CD-group effect sizes, p values, or directions for the Sample 1 title and design tasks. Those task-specific reported statistics and directions are null (p. 11). The AI-versus-solo similarity effects belong to S1-O2.

contrasts.control_arm: Below task-level median CD (title; observed group)
contrasts.locator: p. 11, Creative Direction Reduces the Homogenization Effect; p. 18, Homogenization Analysis

contrasts.control_arm: Below task-level median CD (design; observed group)

diversity_detail.metric: Each participant's mean cosine similarity to other participants in the same CD group and task; lower similarity means greater diversity.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Within each task, all pairs of AI-assisted outputs belonging to the same observed above- or below-median CD group; average each participant's similarities to other group members.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Welch's t-test over participant-level mean within-group similarity scores; between-group Cohen's d uses the pooled sample standard deviation (p. 18, Homogenization Analysis).

studies.label: Sample 2: measured Creative Direction during ChatGPT-assisted personal writing

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants completed the same ChatGPT-assisted writing tasks; there was no contrasting allocation of AI access. Creative Direction was measured from transcripts. Above/below-median Creative Direction groups were formed from observed task-level scores, rather than assigned AI configurations. Separate unassisted ability assessments were predictors, not a no-AI writing arm.

studies.label: Sample 3: preregistered observational replication with Gemini-assisted personal writing

assignment.what_was_assigned: All participants completed the Gemini-assisted tasks. Creative Direction was measured from transcripts; the preregistered diversity comparison split observed scores above/below the task-level median. No random allocation to different AI-assistance conditions is described.

assignment.what_was_assigned: No experimental assignment: existing naturalistic ChatGPT conversations were filtered for creative tasks and a scorable product. Creative Direction was scored from observed interactions, and conversations were aggregated by hashed-IP user identifiers.
assignment.quote: The final analysis sample retained only conversations classified as unambiguous creative tasks, excluding non-creative and ambiguous categories.
assignment.locator: pp. 40–41, Supplementary Information, Sample 4 Methods: Source Dataset, Filtering and Classification Pipeline, and Final Analytic Sample; p. 42, User-Level Aggregation

arms.name: Naturalistic ChatGPT creative conversations
arms.description: Single observational corpus; the count is users with a scorable product, identified through hashed IP addresses.

participants.who: WildChat users pursuing their own creative projects. The paper reports 1,941 unique users in product-creativity analyses, inferred from hashed IPs; it explicitly notes that shared or multiple IPs make this an imperfect proxy for people. The broader corpus has 2,053 user identifiers and 6,290 conversations; the product-scored subset has 5,772 conversations. The analyzed people field preserves the paper's reported user-level count, not a verified count of distinct individuals.
participants.quote: All predictive validity and discriminant validity analyses use this filtered sample (1,941 unique users) unless otherwise noted.
participants.locator: pp. 17–18, Materials and Methods: Sample 4; p. 41, Final Analytic Sample; p. 42, User-Level Aggregation; p. 43, Table S6

ai_tool.how_used: Naturally occurring creative chats in WildChat. The paper selected a product-containing assistant turn from the interaction for scoring because users did not separately submit final products (pp. 40–42).

task.description: Naturalistic creative writing, including stories, scripts, fan fiction, worldbuilding, poems, songs, and letters. Model judges selected a product turn, which was scored for novelty and effectiveness (p. 42, Process and Product Scoring in WildChat).

outcomes.name: WildChat product creativity associated with measured Creative Direction
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Final product creativity is the mean of GPT-4.1, Qwen 3.5-397B, and Grok-3 ratings on a 10–50 scale anchored by novelty and effectiveness (p. 16, Product Creativity Scoring; pp. 28–29, Product Scoring: Creativity). Creative Direction (CD) is scored separately from the chat transcript by a different ensemble of models; primary correlations use mean CD and mean creativity per participant/user (pp. 16, 18). WildChat products are assistant turns selected by majority vote of model judges, rather than separately submitted user responses. Product-scored conversations are aggregated by hashed-IP user identifier, an imperfect proxy for a distinct person (pp. 41–42). Model-version robustness: at the user level, CD–creativity r = .178 (p < .001, N = 1,401) among primarily GPT-3.5-turbo users and r = .195 (p < .001, N = 540) among GPT-4 users; controlling each user's proportion of GPT-4 conversations gives partial r = .181 (p < .001, N = 1,941). The observational conversation-level model comparison reports creativity M = 35.8 for GPT-4 versus 24.9 for GPT-3.5-turbo, d = 1.45; model use was not assigned. These are robustness analyses of the same outcome, distinct from the main user-level CD association (p. 45, Robustness Across GPT Model Versions; Table S9 reports observation-level variants).

contrasts.reported: User-level measured-CD association: r = .28, N = 1,941 (pp. 7–8). Table S5 gives zero-order r = +.281 and partial r = +.282, both p < .001; the partial correlation controls interaction quantity. Users are hashed-IP proxies and CD is observed, not assigned.
contrasts.locator: pp. 7–8, Creative Direction Robustly Predicts Creative Performance; p. 18, Analysis; p. 42, Table S5 and User-Level Aggregation

outcomes.name: WildChat output diversity by measured Creative Direction after restricting repeat users
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Repeat-user robustness restricts the sample to users with only one conversation per IP. The pooled CD–similarity association is nonsignificant, and the restricted sample size is not reported (p. 11; pp. 45–46). Products are model-selected assistant turns and users are hashed-IP proxies (p. 42); this is an observational association.

contrasts.reported: Restricted to users with only one conversation per IP, pooled CD–similarity association: d = 0.06, p = .31 (nonsignificant). Restricted sample size is not reported (n_units = null). No assigned treatment/control arms or task-specific effect sizes are supplied.
contrasts.locator: p. 11, Creative Direction Reduces the Homogenization Effect; pp. 45–46, Repeat-User Robustness of WildChat Homogenization Results

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of product embeddings; reported robustness statistic is the pooled CD–similarity association.
diversity_detail.computed_over: WildChat product turns, restricting the robustness analysis to users with only one conversation per hashed IP (pp. 45–46). The general method describes within-task, within-CD-group pairwise similarity and user-level aggregation (p. 18); the restricted pooling and group construction are not separately detailed.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: A pooled d and p value are reported. The restricted WildChat analysis does not specify its pooling or uncertainty procedure (pp. 45–46); the Welch tests for the controlled task-level CD groups are not assumed to establish this procedure.
diversity_detail.notes: Restricted sample size is not stated, so n_units remains null; the overall 1,941-user creativity count does not supply it. Unit denotes hashed-IP user proxies, with one retained conversation per IP in this analysis. The printed d is retained without sign reversal; there is no clear diversity difference. Selected assistant turns and imperfect user identifiers limit comparability with participant-submitted controlled-task outputs.

company_involvement.description: R.E.B. (Roger E. Beaty) reports support from Amazon, alongside National Science Foundation support. The authors declare no competing interests. A company role in study design, analysis, or reporting is not specified.

eligibility.reason: Sample 1 has an AI-versus-solo within-person comparison, but the full text and supplement state only counterbalancing, not random assignment of condition order (p. 33, Sample 1 Methods; p. 16, Sample 1). Counterbalancing alone does not establish randomized order, so criterion 1 is unclear and design_class is other, not a confirmed RCT or confirmed non-random experiment. Sample 1 analyzed 234 people (p. 43, Table S6) and scored their final outputs for creativity (pp. 10, 16, 35), meeting criteria 2 and 3; under the short-screening rule, core is unclear and this paper goes to the two-screener pipeline. Samples 2 and 3 analyze measured Creative Direction under common AI access and observed median-split groups (pp. 17–18, 35, 37–38); Sample 4 uses existing naturalistic chats (pp. 40–42). Those associations are observational context and do not establish a randomized AI-assistance effect.

one_line_finding: Greater measured Creative Direction was associated with higher product creativity across the four samples (fixed-effects meta-analytic r = .28, 95% CI [.25, .32], reported N = 2,537, including hashed-IP user proxies; p. 8, Figure 2; p. 42, User-Level Aggregation), while random allocation of Sample 1's counterbalanced AI-versus-solo order remains unstated (p. 33).
